title: The mystery of love
hook: love doesn't explain suffering, but it enters it

segments.voice: Yesterday, love is stronger: neither death, nor life, shall be able to separate us from the love of God. Your line was love is stronger. What was the one act of love you did? Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.

"Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Two sisters say those exact words to Jesus, one after the other, in John's Gospel. Martha says it on the road. Mary says it at his feet. It's an accusation and a prayer at the same time, a sentence grief knows in many versions: where were you? You could have stopped this. Why didn't you? Their brother Lazarus has been in the tomb for days. Jesus is standing in front of them. And what he does next is not what anyone writing a neat answer to suffering would have him do. Today: the mystery of love.
screen: `MARTHA ON THE ROAD, MARY AT HIS FEET.`

segments.voice: He doesn't explain. Earlier in the chapter, John has Jesus tell his disciples that Lazarus is asleep and that he is going to wake him. He knows how this story ends. And still, when he sees Mary weeping, and the neighbors who came to mourn with her weeping, the text says he groaned in the spirit and was troubled. The King James uses the same English word, groan, as Romans 8 two days ago, now for Jesus himself. Then he asks one question: "Where have ye laid him?" Not why. Where. Take me to the place it hurts. They say, come and see. And then the verse that in the King James is only two words: "Jesus wept." The people standing there read it the simplest way: "Behold how he loved him!" That's the mystery. Christians have offered reflections on why there is suffering, and some readers say none of them quite closes the question. What the Gospel gives instead is a God who walks into the grief. John's Gospel opens the same way: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." The prophet Isaiah said of God and his people: "In all their affliction he was afflicted." Love doesn't stand outside the pain with an explanation. It asks where, and it goes there. This week walked through that. Clay jars carrying light. Affliction weighed against glory. Comfort passed on. Darkness that isn't dark to God. The Spirit's groan. Love stronger than death. And today, the center of it: love that enters.

Here's the practice: enter someone's pain. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who is hurting right now. Notice the urge to explain it, to fix it, to find the bright side. Set that down. Instead, ask the question Jesus asked: where? Where does it hurt for them? What is the room they're sitting in? Just picture yourself going in and sitting down, without a speech. If you pray, you can pray for them simply by name. If you don't, hold them quietly. When the bell ends, decide one way to go into that room for real. The bell holds the time.
The mystery of love. Love that doesn't explain suffering, but enters it: Jesus at the tomb of his friend, asking where, and weeping.
Your line: love enters. Today, with someone who's hurting, ask a question instead of giving an answer, and then just listen. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Some churches read the raising of Lazarus in John 11 at funerals or in Lent, and churches encourage sitting with the grieving, visiting the sick, and simply being present, as a way of following Jesus into other people's pain.

fork.setup: you're Jesus. Mary falls at your feet, weeping: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." the mourners are weeping with her. what do you do?
options: ask where they've laid him, and weep.
tell her to stop crying, because he'll live.
fork.reveal: he groans in the spirit, asks "where have ye laid him?", and "Jesus wept." the explanation never comes. the presence does.

trapdoor: what you thought: God owes us an explanation for suffering.
what it means: in John 11, Jesus doesn't explain the grief; he asks where it is, goes there, and weeps.
what a scholar hears: John has Jesus say beforehand that he will wake Lazarus, so the tears aren't for lack of hope; they're love, entering the room.

notes: John 11:36 in the KJV reads 'Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him!'; the script calls them 'the people standing there' and 'the neighbors who came to mourn', who are sympathetic in the text. Keeper to confirm the wording.
Isaiah 63:9 has a known textual variant (Hebrew ketiv/qere: 'he was afflicted' vs 'he was not afflicted'); the KJV wording is quoted. Keeper may want a note or a different verse.
'Their brother has been in the tomb for days' paraphrases John 11:17 (four days) without the number.
